paper.title: OpenDeepThink: Parallel Reasoning via Bradley--Terry Aggregation
paper.abstract: Test-time compute scaling is a primary axis for improving LLM reasoning. Existing methods primarily scale depth by extending a single reasoning trace. Scaling breadth by sampling multiple candidates in parallel is straightforward, but introduces a selection bottleneck: choosing the best candidate without a ground-truth verifier, since pointwise LLM judging is noisy and biased. To address this, we introduce OpenDeepThink, a population-based test-time compute framework that selects via pairwise Bradley-Terry comparison. Each generation, the LLM judges random pairs of candidates and aggregates votes via Bradley-Terry into a global ranking; top-ranked candidates are preserved and the top three quarters are mutated using the natural-language critiques produced during comparison; the bottom quarter is discarded. OpenDeepThink raises Gemini 3.1 Pro's effective Codeforces Elo by +405 points in eight sequential LLM-call rounds (~27 minutes wall-clock). The pipeline transfers across weaker and stronger models without retuning, and on the multi-domain HLE benchmark, gains appear concentrated in objectively verifiable domains and reverse in subjective ones. We release CF-73, a curated set of 73 expert-rated Codeforces problems with International Grandmaster annotation and 99% local-evaluation agreement against the official verdict.

sections.abstract: Test-time compute scaling is a primary axis for improving LLM reasoning. Existing methods primarily scale depth by extending a single reasoning trace. Scaling breadth by sampling multiple candidates in parallel is straightforward, but introduces a selection bottleneck: choosing the best candidate without a ground-truth verifier, since pointwise LLM judging is noisy and biased. To address this, we introduce OpenDeepThink, a population-based test-time compute framework that selects via pairwise Bradley-Terry comparison. Each generation, the LLM judges random pairs of candidates and aggregates votes via Bradley-Terry into a global ranking; top-ranked candidates are preserved and the top three quarters are mutated using the natural-language critiques produced during comparison; the bottom quarter is discarded. OpenDeepThink raises Gemini 3.1 Pro's effective Codeforces Elo by +405 points in eight sequential LLM-call rounds (~27 minutes wall-clock). The pipeline transfers across weaker and stronger models without retuning, and on the multi-domain HLE benchmark, gains appear concentrated in objectively verifiable domains and reverse in subjective ones. We release CF-73, a curated set of 73 expert-rated Codeforces problems with International Grandmaster annotation and 99% local-evaluation agreement against the official verdict.

significance.justification: The paper addresses a concrete bottleneck in parallel test-time compute scaling (selection without ground-truth verifiers) and demonstrates substantial gains (+405 Elo on Codeforces), directly informing decisions about whether to parallelize reasoning and how to aggregate multiple candidates.

novelty.justification: The core contribution—applying Bradley-Terry aggregation over pairwise LLM comparisons to drive population-based evolution without external verifiers—is a meaningful combination of existing techniques (pairwise judging, BT ranking, evolutionary algorithms) applied in a novel way to the test-time compute problem, though each component has precedent.

reproducibility.justification: The paper provides full algorithm pseudocode, complete prompt templates, hyperparameter specifications, and releases code at a public GitHub repository; the main friction is the substantial per-problem API cost (~285 calls) and dependence on Gemini models, but the method is clearly implementable.

clarity.justification: The paper is well-structured with clear motivation, algorithm, and ablations; the writing is precise and the figures effectively illustrate the pipeline; minor overclaim in abstract (gains 'transfer' to weaker/stronger models) is tempered by honest discussion of limitations and domain-specific failure modes on HLE.

topical_fit.justification: Directly addresses a core decision for LLM system builders—how to allocate test-time compute across parallel reasoning paths and select among candidates—with practical validation on competitive programming and multi-domain reasoning, making it squarely in the applied LLM builder sweet spot.

draft.post_text:
Running the same LLM against itself as a tournament judge raises Gemini 3.1 Pro's competitive programming score by 405 Elo points in under 30 minutes.

Researchers at UC San Diego built OpenDeepThink, a framework that runs many candidate solutions in parallel and selects among them using pairwise comparisons aggregated via Bradley-Terry, a ranking method that infers global standings from head-to-head votes. The system uses the same model to generate and judge, requires no external verifier, and completes in eight sequential LLM-call rounds at roughly 285 API calls per problem.

The core finding is about selection, not generation. On a controlled 500-pair diagnostic, pairwise judgment reached 86% accuracy versus 59% for the standard approach of scoring each solution in isolation. The gap persists even after giving the pointwise baseline its own refinement budget. Gains on the multi-domain HLE benchmark concentrate in objectively verifiable domains and reverse in subjective ones, which is a candid signal about where the method's soft verifier actually holds.

For teams scaling LLM inference, the practical implication is that how you pick among parallel outputs matters as much as how many you generate. The framework is training-free and transferred across Gemini Flash and Gemini 2.5 Pro without retuning, though the per-problem cost of 285 API calls will be prohibitive for latency-sensitive workloads.

Worth reading if you are designing evaluation or selection layers for LLM pipelines; worth setting aside if your bottleneck is cost rather than accuracy.

Paper: OpenDeepThink: Parallel Reasoning via Bradley-Terry Aggregation, Zhou et al.
